name: Urinary Tract Infections: Cystitis, Prostatitis, and Pyelonephritis

clinicalPearls: UTI denotes symptomatic infection somewhere along the urinary tract; bacteria in urine WITHOUT related symptoms is asymptomatic bacteriuria (ASB), not UTI, and generally should NOT be treated (Harrison 22e p.1086).

Treatment of ASB is discouraged except in two settings: pregnancy (untreated ASB is linked to pyelonephritis, preterm delivery, and low birth weight) and before urologic procedures causing mucosal injury such as lithotripsy or transurethral prostate resection (Harrison 22e p.1086).

Cystitis presents with dysuria, frequency, and urgency, often with suprapubic discomfort, new nocturia, hesitancy, or gross hematuria; fever, rigors, and unilateral flank/back pain are INCONSISTENT with uncomplicated cystitis and point to infection beyond the bladder (Harrison 22e p.1088).

Fever is a key feature distinguishing cystitis from pyelonephritis; mild pyelonephritis may show only low-grade fever with or without costovertebral angle pain, while severe disease brings high fever, rigors, nausea, vomiting, and flank pain (Harrison 22e p.1089).

E. coli is the predominant uropathogen across UTI syndromes, accounting for roughly 75-90% of acute cystitis isolates; Staphylococcus saprophyticus causes about 5-15% (more in younger women) (Harrison 22e p.1087).

Isolation of S. aureus or Salmonella from urine should raise suspicion of concomitant bacteremia, since hematogenous seeding (<2% of UTIs) typically involves these more virulent organisms (Harrison 22e p.1088).

Acute bacterial prostatitis (ABP) is a typically severe illness with dysuria, frequency, and prostatic/pelvic/perineal pain, sometimes with fever, rigors, or bladder outlet obstruction; chronic bacterial prostatitis (CBP) presents insidiously as recurrent cystitis episodes, often without systemic signs (Harrison 22e p.1088).

Chronic pelvic pain syndrome (formerly chronic prostatitis) is far more common than bacterial prostatitis, is NOT associated with bacteriuria, and does NOT improve with antibiotics; obtaining urine cultures in male UTI helps distinguish these entities (Harrison 22e p.1088).

Diagnostic stewardship - not culturing urine in patients lacking UTI signs/symptoms (except pregnancy or pre-urologic-procedure screening) - is the key intervention to reduce misdiagnosis and overtreatment of ASB (Harrison 22e p.1088).

In catheterized patients bacteriuria and pyuria are essentially inevitable, so an abnormal urinalysis alone cannot diagnose CAUTI; localizing or systemic symptoms must be present and other causes excluded (Harrison 22e p.1090).

Recurrent UTI is not automatically 'complicated' - individual episodes can be uncomplicated; early recurrence (within 2 weeks) is usually relapse rather than reinfection and should prompt a search for a sequestered focus (Harrison 22e pp.1086-1087).
harrison.pathophysiology: The urinary tract behaves as a continuous column of urine from kidney to urethra. Most UTIs arise by ascending infection: periurethral and vaginal-introital colonization by intestinal flora (usually E. coli) is the critical first step, followed by ascent up the urethra to the bladder and, in renal infection, up the ureter to the kidney. Hematogenous seeding accounts for less than 2% of UTIs and usually involves virulent organisms (e.g., S. aureus, Salmonella). Outcome depends on the interplay of host, pathogen, and environmental factors. The flushing action of normal voiding clears bacteria; urinary stasis, obstruction, foreign bodies (stones, catheters), and biofilm formation favor infection. Uropathogenic E. coli express virulence factors: type 1 pili bind mannose on bladder uroepithelium to initiate cystitis, while P fimbriae bind the P blood-group antigen on renal epithelium and are important in pyelonephritis and bloodstream invasion; toxins, iron-acquisition systems, biofilms, and capsules also contribute. Host susceptibility has a hereditary component (familial/maternal history; non-secretor blood-group phenotypes increasing E. coli adherence; Toll-like receptor and IL-8 receptor gene variants). Disruption of vaginal lactobacilli (spermicide/nonoxynol-9, menopausal atrophy) promotes E. coli colonization (Harrison 22e pp.1087-1088).
additionalDifferentials: Asymptomatic bacteriuria (positive culture without localizing symptoms)
Sexually transmitted infections - urethritis/cervicitis from Chlamydia trachomatis, Neisseria gonorrhoeae, Mycoplasma genitalium
infectionMimics: Cervicitis due to Chlamydia trachomatis or Neisseria gonorrhoeae
nonInfectiousMimics: Chronic pelvic pain syndrome (noninfectious prostatic pain without bacteriuria)
Delirium from non-urinary causes mislabeled as UTI in older adults with incidental ASB
additionalInvestigations: Urine dipstick for nitrite and leukocyte esterase (best used to help rule out UTI; only Enterobacterales convert nitrate to nitrite, so non-Enterobacterales and dilute frequently-voided urine can be falsely negative)
Microscopic urinalysis for pyuria and hematuria

Urine culture with susceptibilities - warranted in pregnancy, suspected resistant organisms, recurrent or complicated UTI, and all male UTI; ASB screening in pregnancy must use culture because dipstick is not sufficiently sensitive
Blood cultures when fever or systemic signs suggest infection beyond the bladder

Imaging (CT or ultrasound) in men with febrile UTI (even first episode) to evaluate for obstruction or anatomic abnormality; suspect intraparenchymal abscess with persistent fever/bacteremia despite therapy
Urologic consultation for unclear diagnosis or recurrent UTI in men
redFlags: Fever, rigors, or unilateral flank/back pain in a patient with urinary symptoms (suggests pyelonephritis, prostatitis, or bloodstream involvement)
Severe pyelonephritis with high fever, rigors, nausea, vomiting, and flank pain
Emphysematous pyelonephritis (gas in renal/perinephric tissue), occurring almost exclusively in poorly controlled diabetes
Acute papillary necrosis causing obstructive uropathy; bilateral papillary necrosis may present with rapidly rising serum creatinine
Continued fever and/or bacteremia despite antibiotics (suggests intraparenchymal renal abscess)
Signs of sepsis in an older patient with altered mentation
S. aureus or Salmonella in urine (consider concomitant bacteremia and metastatic prostatic focus)
Bladder outlet obstruction with acute bacterial prostatitis
harrison.prognosis: UTI is common and patients typically respond favorably and rapidly to appropriately chosen modern antimicrobials. Uncomplicated cystitis in low-risk women carries a low risk of serious complications and can often be managed remotely. About 20-30% of women with one UTI develop recurrences (average ~2.6 reinfections/year; rate 0.3-7.6 per patient-year), with likelihood of recurrence decreasing as time since the last infection lengthens. Up to 80% of women have at least one UTI in their lifetime; lifetime prevalence in U.S. men is about 14%. Untreated ASB in pregnancy carries risk of pyelonephritis, preterm delivery, and low birth weight. Xanthogranulomatous pyelonephritis causes suppurative destruction of renal tissue and its mass effect can mimic renal malignancy (Harrison 22e pp.1086-1089).
pitfalls: Diagnosing UTI from pyuria/bacteriuria alone without requiring symptoms - this conflates ASB with true UTI; degree of pyuria in an asymptomatic patient should not drive the diagnosis (very high pyuria is common with urinary stasis, ESRD, or obstructed catheters).
Treating ASB outside pregnancy or pre-urologic-procedure settings - it does not reduce future UTIs and may even increase infection risk (e.g., in renal transplant recipients).

Premature diagnostic closure: attributing an older patient's isolated altered mentation to 'UTI' without excluding sepsis and other time-sensitive causes of delirium; a reported history of recurrent UTIs may actually reflect persistent ASB.

Relying on a negative dipstick to rule out UTI - false negatives occur with non-Enterobacterales organisms, dilute frequently-voided urine, and it is insufficiently sensitive to exclude bacteriuria in pregnancy.
Mistaking an STI (especially C. trachomatis) for UTI, or treating dysuria due to vaginitis/cervicitis as UTI; vaginal discharge should prompt STI evaluation.
Assuming all male UTI is 'complicated' or that complicated-UTI guidelines apply to prostatitis; not all men with UTI have urinary tract abnormalities, especially those 45 years or younger.
Misinterpreting a mixed-flora culture as infection - usually contamination except in long-term catheterization, chronic retention, or urinary-enteric/genital fistula.
harrison.severityClassification: Clinical syndrome-based: asymptomatic bacteriuria (ASB) vs symptomatic UTI. Uncomplicated UTI = infection confined to the bladder (cystitis) in a woman or man without a urinary catheter. Complicated UTI = infection extending beyond the bladder (prostatitis, pyelonephritis, bacteremia) or in the setting of catheterization (CAUTI). Pyelonephritis is graded clinically from mild (low-grade fever +/- back/CVA pain) to severe (high fever, rigors, nausea, vomiting, flank pain). Severe/special forms: emphysematous pyelonephritis and xanthogranulomatous pyelonephritis. Lab/diagnostic thresholds: pyuria conventionally >10 WBCs/HPF (poor specificity ~36%; a cutoff nearer 250 WBCs/HPF correlates better with symptoms in older women); for women with cystitis symptoms a colony count >10^2 bacteria/mL is more sensitive (95%) than the classic 10^5/mL; CAUTI bacteriuria threshold is >=10^3 CFU/mL (Harrison 22e pp.1086-1092).
